title: Visual thought experiment: The Inherited Promise
tests: Core concept: identity and moral continuity after copying. Exact question: If every copy wakes up believing it is you, which one inherits your promise? Visual mechanism: one original holds one brass token while four identical copies each reach from a separate sleeper carriage beside an identical sealed envelope. Capture/style logic: photorealistic large-format architectural scene at blue hour, high three-quarter view, wet circular station and four branching tracks. Anti-repeat variables: railway topology, clone-choice ethics, elderly Black woman with silver braid, rust-red/bottle-green/amber/indigo palette, split-flap architectural typography, single-token contradiction.
prompt:
Create a finished square photorealistic visual thought experiment titled "The Inherited Promise." The exact philosophical question is: "If every copy wakes up believing it is you, which one inherits your promise?" Make that exact sentence clearly readable, verbatim, as the only substantial typography in the image, cleanly illuminated in a single restrained amber split-flap station display suspended above the scene. Do not add an answer or any other readable text.

Stage the thought experiment on a monumental circular railway platform at blue hour. One elderly Black woman with a long silver natural braid, deep brown skin, a thoughtful weathered face, and a rust-red traveling coat stands at the center where four wet tracks branch toward four different dark tunnels. Four identical bottle-green sleeper carriages wait on the branches. Through each carriage window sits a materially perfect copy of the same woman—same face, braid, coat, age, and expression—already awake and reaching one empty hand toward the original. Beside every seated copy lies the same sealed ivory envelope. The standing original has only one small brass promise-token resting in her open palm. Make the single token, four requesting hands, and four identical envelopes the decisive visual contradiction: each copy remembers making the same promise, but only one token can be given.

Use a high three-quarter wide architectural camera that clearly shows the circular platform, central original, four separate carriages, four branching tracks, and four tunnels without resembling a poster or diagram. Build tactile physical credibility with rain-dark black stone, iron rail webs, aged brass trim, bottle-green enamel, cream linen curtains, amber carriage lamps, cold indigo skylight, steam near the wheels, rain beads on windows, damp footprints leading only to the central woman, fine wool fibers, scratched paint, oxidized rivets, wet reflections, and subtle depth in the vaulted station. The copies must look genuinely identical to the original, not merely similar strangers; keep all poses calm, natural, serious, and emotionally restrained. The scene should invite interpretation about identity and moral continuity without answering the question.

No laboratory, cloning pods, humanoid robots, holograms, glowing circuits, cyberpunk neon, code, mirrors substituting for the copies, horror, body distortion, extra people, duplicate limbs, comedy, costumes, explanatory captions, speech bubbles, logos, watermark, flat quote-card composition, paper poster, or illegible question. The exact sentence on the split-flap display must read: "If every copy wakes up believing it is you, which one inherits your promise?"

Reusable prompt template: Stage the question "[EXACT QUESTION]" as a physically coherent visual thought experiment in [SETTING]. Show [ONE PERSON OR SUBJECT] confronting [PRECISE CONTRADICTION OR CHOICE], integrate the exact question as the only substantial readable text on [ARCHITECTURAL TEXT SURFACE], and use [MATERIALS], [LIGHTING], and [CAMERA] to invite interpretation without answering it.

Example substitution: [EXACT QUESTION] = If every copy wakes up believing it is you, which one inherits your promise?; [SETTING] = a rain-dark circular railway platform at blue hour; [ONE PERSON OR SUBJECT] = one elderly Black woman with a silver braid and rust-red coat; [PRECISE CONTRADICTION OR CHOICE] = four identical copies each remember the same promise but only one brass token exists; [ARCHITECTURAL TEXT SURFACE] = an amber split-flap display; [MATERIALS] = wet black stone, bottle-green enamel, aged brass, cream linen, steam and rain beads; [LIGHTING] = cold indigo skylight with amber carriage lamps; [CAMERA] = high three-quarter wide architectural view.

title: Visual thought experiment: The Answer Before the Question
tests: Exact question: If your answer arrives before the question, who made the choice? | Core concept: causal agency under backward evidence | Staged contradiction: sealed crimson answer capsule has arrived while all three question plungers remain raised and safety-wired | Capture logic: high three-quarter large-format architectural photograph | Materials: dark oak, oxidized brass, cream ceramic, hand-blown glass, slate, copper, linen | Anti-repeat: analog pneumatic decision chamber, pre-arrived answer, single young South Asian man, crimson/cobalt/amber mechanism
prompt:
Create a finished square photorealistic visual thought experiment titled "The Answer Before the Question." The exact philosophical question is: "If your answer arrives before the question, who made the choice?" Render that exact sentence clearly and verbatim as the only substantial typography, illuminated within one long ivory-glass architectural frieze above the scene. Do not add an answer, labels, numbers, logos, or any other readable text.

Stage the thought experiment inside a monumental analog decision chamber at cold dawn. At the center stands a young South Asian man in his late twenties, medium-brown skin, lean build, angular face, dense curly black hair, clean-shaven, wearing a plain slate-blue wool work coat. He is calm and serious, one hand hovering naturally above three large unpressed question plungers arranged in a shallow arc: cobalt ceramic, amber ceramic, and crimson ceramic. Make all three plungers visibly untouched, fully raised, and still secured by intact hair-thin brass safety wires.

Behind each plunger, a matching transparent pneumatic return tube descends from the high vaulted machinery. The cobalt and amber return trays are empty. In the crimson return tray, however, one sealed crimson glass answer capsule has already arrived; condensation clings to it and a faint trail of fresh frost runs backward up the crimson tube. The matching crimson plunger remains raised with its safety wire intact. Make this single pre-arrived capsule, the untouched controls, and the hovering hand the decisive causal contradiction. The scene must invite the viewer to wonder whether the future answer caused the choice or the choice caused the answer, without resolving it.

Use a high three-quarter wide architectural camera that clearly shows the man, all three raised plungers, all three return tubes, the lone crimson capsule, and the question frieze in one coherent physical space. Compose a triangular flow from the hovering hand through the crimson capsule up the frosted return tube, with the other two empty systems framing it symmetrically. Build rich material credibility with dark quarter-sawn oak consoles, oxidized brass pipework, cream ceramic insulators, thick hand-blown glass tubes, slate floor tiles, braided linen seals, cast-iron arches, copper pressure vessels, small mechanical shutters with unreadable blank faces, worn handrails, tiny valve wheels, rivets, gasket seams, glass bubbles, fingerprints on polished brass, condensation beads, frost crystals, dust in dawn shafts, and restrained amber service lamps.

Palette: deep oak brown, tarnished brass green, cream ceramic, slate blue, cobalt, amber, one concentrated crimson accent, cold silver dawn, and warm low service light. Render it like a large-format photograph of an impossible but materially believable civic mechanism, contemplative and serious, with crisp readable causal staging, realistic depth, tactile surfaces, and no theatrical spectacle.

No screens, holograms, code, circuits, robots, humanoid machines, glowing brains, cyberpunk neon, clocks, mirrors, duplicates, extra people, horror, body distortion, comedy, magic effects, multiple anomalies, explanatory arrows, diagrams, paper, posters, quote-card layout, captions, labels, watermarks, or illegible question. The exact sentence on the ivory-glass frieze must read: "If your answer arrives before the question, who made the choice?"

Reusable prompt template: Stage the question "[EXACT QUESTION]" as a physically coherent visual thought experiment in [SETTING]. Show [SUBJECT] confronting [PRECISE CAUSAL CONTRADICTION], integrate the exact question as the only substantial readable text on [ARCHITECTURAL TEXT SURFACE], and use [MATERIALS], [LIGHTING], and [CAMERA] to invite interpretation without answering it.

Example substitution: [EXACT QUESTION] = If your answer arrives before the question, who made the choice?; [SETTING] = a monumental analog decision chamber at cold dawn; [SUBJECT] = a young South Asian man in a slate-blue wool work coat; [PRECISE CAUSAL CONTRADICTION] = one crimson answer capsule has already arrived although all three question plungers remain raised and safety-wired; [ARCHITECTURAL TEXT SURFACE] = a long illuminated ivory-glass frieze; [MATERIALS] = dark oak, oxidized brass, cream ceramic, hand-blown glass, slate, copper, and linen seals; [LIGHTING] = cold silver dawn with restrained amber service lamps; [CAMERA] = high three-quarter wide architectural view.
